overview: Double-crested cormorants are fish-eating water birds protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, a law that generally bars killing or capturing migratory birds without federal permission. This bill would require the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, part of the Interior Department, to issue rules within a year setting up regional plans for controlling cormorants, worked out with the four regional flyway councils that coordinate migratory bird management. The plans would spell out when and how cormorants may be killed or otherwise controlled, who may do it (such as state and tribal wildlife agencies and licensed lake and pond managers), required non-lethal measures, and public yearly reports on how many birds are taken. They must keep cormorant populations at sustainable levels and consider the birds' effects on fisheries, plants, other birds, water quality, and endangered species. The agency would survey the population and update the plans every five years, report on the idea of hunting licenses for cormorants, and the law would end on January 1, 2034. As of October 29, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar for a vote.
for: Supporters say cormorants can do real damage to fish farms, sport fisheries, and island habitats, and that regional plans give states, tribes, and landowners clearer and faster ways to deal with documented problems.
against: Critics say widening who can kill a protected bird, including private lake and pond managers and possibly hunters, risks overkilling cormorants and harming other birds, and that blame for fish losses is not always well established.
